transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luke (Redwood SE), Nora (CTO VerdantOps), Rajesh (Platform), Aisha (SRE), Evan (Product), Sam (procurement)

Summary: High-level qualify for Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU) — VerdantOps currently on self-hosted model but exploring move to Redwood Dedicated for predictable latency and isolation. Key concerns: tenant isolation, burst to hosted fallback, KMS & audit logs, prewarm/warm pool behavior, expected QPS and tail latency.
Topics: reserved capacity sizing, isolation (node-level vs tenant fencing), burst model & warm pool, VPC/private deployment nuances, timeline and stakeholders, security/compliance checkpoints.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) ---
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking time today. Quick intros, I'm Maya AE on Redwood, Luke is our solutions engineer who will jump into topology and perf. Over to you Nora for a quick overview of why VerdantOps is exploring reserves.
[00:14] Nora (CTO): Yeah thanks Maya. Um, short story is that our inference costs and tail latency have been painful during peaks. We currently run self-hosted on mixed spot/ondemand and have a lot of variance. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated to get predictable throughput and also because of the compliance side — audit logs, KMS, and isolation.
[00:34] Luke (SE): Appreciate the context. Rajesh, can you talk expected load shapes? Peak QPS, percent of long sequences, etc?
[00:42] Rajesh (Platform Eng): Sure — rough numbers: steady-state about 6–8 QPS, spikes up to 75 QPS for short windows (5–15 minutes) during product events. Token lengths are usually small, median 20 tokens, but heavy tail where some calls request 2–3k tokens for summarization jobs. So we need both low p50 latency for chat flows and ability to handle those long seq jobs without blowing OOMs.
[01:08] Aisha (SRE): Also important, we can't have noisy neighbor that affects our production tenant. We need strong tenant isolation — ideally dedicated nodes or physical segregation, not just cgroups.
[01:18] Maya (AE): Got it. For Dedicated we offer reserved GPU pools and options for tenant fencing. We can map customers to reserved pools that won't be shared or we can allocate per-tenant pinned nodes — there's cost tradeoff.
[01:28] Evan (Product): Timeline wise, we want decision in next 6 weeks and POC within April if numbers look ok. Procurement here is conservative so Sam is on to check purchasing cadence.
[01:40] Sam (procurement): For PO we need SLA language, basic compliance pack (SOC2 Type II), and a price band.
[01:46] Maya (AE): We will share SOC2 and a compliance bundle link.

[02:00] Luke (SE): A couple technical clarifications — when you say long sequences, are those synchronous API calls that hit user-facing latency, or background batch jobs?
[02:08] Rajesh: It's a mix. The 2–3k token summarize jobs are mostly async background, but sometimes product triggers them during onboarding flows — they could be user visible. So we want those to fallback to a background queue if they threaten interactive latency.
[02:22] Luke: That's a common pattern. On Redwood Dedicated we recommend isolating interactive low-latency requests on a warm pool of reserved nodes and routing heavy async to a separate reserved partition or to a queued hosted fallback depending on cost.
[02:36] Nora: Can you explain warm pool vs pre-warmed vs hotpool? I keep seeing those terms in your docs and they blur together.
[02:44] Maya: Sure. Our docs call them warm-pool and hotpool sometimes, sorry for the naming drift in different docs. Briefly: warm-pool are reserved GPUs kept with lower instance density preloaded with model KV cache for fast spin-up; hotpool is essentially fully provisioned ready-to-serve nodes for ultra-low tail latency but higher cost. Prewarm is the act of loading model weights/KV to reduce first-token latency. We will send a concise playbook link after this call.
[03:12] Aisha: From a security perspective we need to ensure KMS integration and audit logs for every inference query — not payload logging but metadata (model used, timestamp, requester). Is that supported in Dedicated?
[03:24] Luke: Yes — Dedicated integrates with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping and provides immutable audit logs with per-request metadata. There's configuration for masking payloads. Some older transcriptions have KMS as K M S, but yes we support common KMS providers and onprem HSMs for Private deployments.
[03:40] Rajesh: Good, also what about network topology — we need VPC peering/no public egress for data in region.
[03:47] Maya: For Redwood Private and Dedicated we offer VPC connectors and private networking — you can pin to a region and we can do AWS VPC endpoints or direct connect alternatives. For customers that need air-gapped onprem we have a Private deployment path.

[04:05] Nora: One of our key blockers is burst — how does Redwood handle bursts beyond our reserved baseline? We need a plan to absorb sudden 3x–5x surges for short windows without SLO violation.
[04:16] Luke: Short answer: multiple layers. First, reserved capacity sized for your baseline interactive QPS to protect p50/p95. Second, warm-pool and hotpool prewarm to keep tail latency low. Third, realtime fallback routing — if reserved is saturated we can route to hosted variants (cheaper but multi-tenant) or spin ephemeral nodes if policy and region capacity permit. Finally, we support request-level throttling and graceful degradation — e.g., route long sequences to background queue or return degraded summarization (shorter length).
[04:48] Aisha: Ephemeral nodes — what's the expected spin-up time? We can't have 2–3 minute spinups for interactive flows.
[04:56] Luke: Ephemeral cold spin is generally minutes; hence we don't rely on cold ephemerals for interactive spikes. That's where warm-pool/hotpool are critical. Warm pool brings p95 down to sub-second for typical models. We also recommend prefix/KV caching at the app layer where possible to avoid repeated long context builds.
[05:18] Rajesh: How do you charge for warm-pool resources? Is it flat reserved monthly or metered per-use when serving?
[05:26] Maya: Reserved capacity has a committed monthly fee per GPU (we'll send banded pricing). Warm-pool is typically included as part of a reserved plan but with configuration options. There's also burst credits and short-term burst billing if you exceed reserved commitment. We'll include detailed TCO examples in the spreadsheet.

[05:44] Evan: Can you do a quick sketch of a recommended topology for our load — keep interactive sub-second, allow async long jobs?
[05:51] Luke: Quick sketch: two reserved partitions — 1) interactive partition: 2–3 prewarmed nodes sized for 75QPS short spikes (autoscaled but reserved), with strict request routing and token limits; 2) batch partition: larger instances optimized for long sequences, scheduled jobs with higher latency tolerance. Policy-level fallback to hosted pool for non-sensitive async workloads. We'll annotate assumptions — e.g., that 75QPS spike is 85% short queries under 50 tokens.
[06:20] Nora: That makes sense. What about model variants and quantization — can you run INT8 or 4-bit variants to reduce memory and cost?
[06:29] Luke: Yes, runtime supports quantized model variants and we can recommend quantization profile per workload. For long sequences you might favor higher precision but we can trade quality vs cost. Our Optimize team can run evals to show output quality delta.

[06:44] Sam: On contracting, what SLA levels do you offer for Dedicated? We need uptime and 95th latency guarantees.
[06:51] Maya: Dedicated has SLA tiers with uptime guarantees and latency targets depending on region and committed capacity. We'll include specific SLA language in the contract packet. Procurement will want remedy terms and termination clauses — Sam, we can follow up with legal.

[07:08] (short cross talk, background noise)
[07:20] Rajesh: If we pin reserved GPUs in us-west-2, but during a major product event that region is constrained, can you failover to another region without data residency impact?
[07:30] Luke: Failover across regions is possible but depends on data residency/regulatory constraints. For strict residency, failover might be limited; for others we can route to a neighboring region with replication of model weights. Also we have model variant fallback: switch to a smaller quantized model in the same region to preserve latency.

[07:58] Aisha: For telemetry, we need per-route latency distributions, token-level cost, and tracing hooks integrated into our observability stack (Datadog).
[08:07] Maya: Console provides per-route dashboards, token-level cost, traces, and we have exporters for Datadog and OpenTelemetry. You'll be able to tag requests with request IDs for end-to-end tracing.

[08:20] Nora: Ok — deep tech question — how does the runtime manage KV cache for long conversations to avoid recompute? Does it persist KV across requests for a user session or is it per-request?
[08:31] Luke: We maintain KV cache per session and we shard across nodes. There's TTLs and eviction policies. For Dedicated we can tune KV cache retention (longer TTLs) because you have reserved memory; in shared hosted you might get shorter TTLs. That change is a big lever for p95/p99 latency.

[08:52] Rajesh: Any caveats around preloading model weights for many variants — memory pressure? If we have a few different model sizes for different product features, will warm pools need X nodes per model?
[09:03] Luke: Correct — warmpool sizing depends on number of model variants kept resident. Each distinct model consumes GPU memory. We can do model multiplexing with memory-aware placement, but it increases cost. We'll provide a sizing worksheet to estimate nodes per model variant and expected warmpool hit rates.

[09:24] Evan: What's the onboarding timeline if we sign a reserved plan — how soon can we get production traffic?
[09:31] Maya: Typical onboarding is 4–8 weeks: contract, infra setup (VPC peering, KMS), warmpool provisioning and prewarm, integration testing, smoke tests, then cutover. Shorter timelines possible if you accept hosted fallback for burst and limit compliance gating.

[09:48] Nora: For the POC we want to validate p95 under our interactive workload and an end-to-end test of burst behavior. Can Redwood run a 48–72 hour synthetic that mirrors our traffic?
[09:58] Luke: Yes, we can run a benchmarking exercise. We'll need an anonymized traffic sample (7-day trace), defined success criteria, and a target SLAs for p95/p99. We'll do both perf and chaos tests (evict nodes) if you want.

[10:12] Aisha: Is there an option to instrument and run chaos tests ourselves in a staging environment?
[10:17] Luke: Absolutely. We'll give access to a staging partition where you can run fault injection. For Dedicated customers we also support a test harness.

[10:26] (brief pause)
[10:32] Maya: Alright, quick recap then next steps. From Redwood side: Maya will send pricing/TCO and warm-pool playbook with links to SOC2 and SLA language. Luke will prepare sizing worksheet and run initial latency/cost model. From VerdantOps: Nora will share anonymized traffic 7-day trace and confirm primary stakeholders.
[10:53] Nora: Yep we'll get the trace over. One Q — when you say warmpool reduces p95 to sub-second, is that for 1k token or small payloads?
[11:03] Luke: For small payloads (sub-100 tokens) warmpool typically yields p95 < 300–600ms depending on model. For 1k+ tokens p95 grows and depends on batch behavior; we'd likely route those to batch partition. We'll detail numbers in the TCO pack.

[11:18] Evan: Can Redwood provide a short list of configuration guardrails we should enforce at the app level to avoid accidental long sync requests?
[11:25] Maya: Yes — rate-limit per user, request token caps, async queues for long jobs, circuit breakers, and sentinel metrics to trigger fallback. We'll include recommended configs.

[11:36] Sam: Procurement question — do you accept monthly invoicing and net-30?
[11:40] Maya: Yes typically net-30, monthly invoicing for usage; reserved commitments invoiced per contract terms. We'll confirm in the pricing doc.

[11:48] Rajesh: Any blockers on our side for Private deployment? We might need onprem air-gap down the road.
[11:55] Luke: Private onprem is supported but has longer lead times for setup and security review — usually multi-month. For initial POC Dedicated with VPC peering is faster.

[12:07] (background chatter, note taking)
[12:12] Nora: One more — does Redwood have a practice for rolling updates of model weights to avoid cache stampede and cold starts during rollout?
[12:20] Luke: Yes, rollouts are canary based with staged pre-warm and KV cache seed strategies. We also offer automatic fallback to prior model if quality regressions occur.

[12:33] Maya: Great. Any outstanding concerns we didn't touch?
[12:37] Aisha: I'd like to review the exact audit log schema and retention controls — send that in the compliance pack.
[12:44] Maya: Will do.

[12:48] Nora: Sounds good. We'll look for the artifacts and sync the deep dive.

[12:54] Luke: I'll prepare the sizing questions so we can run numbers.

[12:58] Maya: OK thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items we summarized.

[13:05] (meeting ends)

Recap (auto):
